title: Strategy and Template Method
scopeHtml: Scope: Strategy and Template Method patterns with before/after refactors, Java and Kotlin, library and Android examples, when not to use.

notes.title: Why behavioral patterns exist
notes.html:
Behavioral patterns are recipes for how objects divide work and talk to each other. Creational patterns say how objects are made, structural ones how they are assembled, behavioral ones how they behave together at runtime. Most of them attack one smell: a giant if/else or switch that keeps growing, or objects that know too much about each other.

The core trick behind almost all of them: replace a conditional with polymorphism, or replace a direct call with an indirection. Instead of "if type is A do this, else if B do that", you hold an object that already knows what to do.

Worked example. A checkout method has 6 payment branches, 40 lines each = 240 lines in one method. Each new payment type edits that method (risk of breaking the other 5). After a pattern: 6 classes of about 40 lines, adding a 7th touches zero existing lines. That is the Open/Closed Principle in numbers.

Industry examples. Java's Comparator (Strategy), RecyclerView.Adapter (Template-ish), LiveData (Observer), OkHttp interceptors (Chain of Responsibility), Android Intent handling and Handler messages (Command-like).

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: the waiter does not cook each dish personally with a giant rulebook; he hands the order to the right station.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting GoF names with no code. Always show a before and after.
  • Applying a pattern where one if is clearer. Patterns have a cost: more classes and more indirection.
  • Confusing look-alikes (Strategy vs State vs Command). The last note of this track compares them.

notes.title: Strategy: the idea
notes.html:
Strategy lets you pick an algorithm at runtime by putting each variant behind the same interface. The caller (the "context") holds a reference to a strategy and delegates. Change the object, change the behaviour, without touching the caller.

Use it when you have several ways to do one job: sort order, pricing rule, compression format, retry policy, route calculation.

+----------------+        +-------------------+
|  Checkout      |------->| <<interface>>     |
| (context)      |        | DiscountStrategy  |
| - strategy     |        | + apply(total)    |
| + pay(total)   |        +---------+---------+
+----------------+                  ^
        +---------------------------+------------------+
        |                           |                  |
 +--------------+          +----------------+  +----------------+
 | NoDiscount   |          | PercentOff     |  | FlatOff        |
 +--------------+          +----------------+  +----------------+

Before (the smell):

class Checkout {
    double pay(double total, String coupon) {
        if (coupon.equals("NONE"))        return total;
        else if (coupon.equals("PERCENT")) return total * 0.9;
        else if (coupon.equals("FLAT"))    return total - 100;
        else throw new IllegalArgumentException(coupon);
    }
}

Every new coupon edits pay. Tests must cover all branches in one method.

After:

interface DiscountStrategy { double apply(double total); }

class PercentOff implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final double pct;
    PercentOff(double pct) { this.pct = pct; }
    public double apply(double total) { return total * (1 - pct); }
}
class FlatOff implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final double amount;
    FlatOff(double amount) { this.amount = amount; }
    public double apply(double total) { return Math.max(0, total - amount); }
}

class Checkout {
    private DiscountStrategy strategy;
    Checkout(DiscountStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }
    void setStrategy(DiscountStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }
    double pay(double total) { return strategy.apply(total); }
}
// new Checkout(new PercentOff(0.10)).pay(1000) -> 900.0

Kotlin variant. A strategy with one method is just a function, so use a function type or fun interface:

fun interface DiscountStrategy { fun apply(total: Double): Double }

class Checkout(private var strategy: DiscountStrategy) {
    fun pay(total: Double) = strategy.apply(total)
}

val tenOff = DiscountStrategy { it * 0.9 }
val flat100 = DiscountStrategy { (it - 100).coerceAtLeast(0.0) }
println(Checkout(tenOff).pay(1000.0)) // 900.0

Decision gravity. Choosing Strategy is reversible and cheap: it is a local refactor behind an interface. The risky part is the interface shape; if two strategies need different inputs (one needs the user, one needs the cart), the interface grows or you pass a context object. Interface changes touch every implementation.

Everyday analogy. Choosing how to get to the airport: taxi, metro or bike. Same goal, interchangeable ways, you pick at departure.

Common interview traps.

  • Strategy vs a plain if: with two stable branches that never change, if is fine.
  • Passing the whole context to every strategy "just in case" couples them to the caller.
  • Who picks the strategy? Say it out loud: a factory, config, or the caller. Often a Map from key to strategy replaces the original if chain.

notes.title: Strategy in real libraries and Android
notes.html:
You already use Strategy daily:

Where Strategy interface Variants
Java collections Comparator<T> Comparator.comparing(...), reversed, custom
java.util.concurrent RejectedExecutionHandler Abort, CallerRuns, Discard
Android layouts RecyclerView.LayoutManager Linear, Grid, StaggeredGrid
Android image loading Glide/Coil Transformation, DiskCacheStrategy circle crop, none/all/automatic
OkHttp / Retrofit Converter.Factory Gson, Moshi, kotlinx.serialization
Spring Security PasswordEncoder BCrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2
Dependency injection Hilt-bound interface Real vs fake in tests

Worked example (retry policy). A client retries failed calls. Strategies: FixedDelay(500ms), ExponentialBackoff(base=200ms, factor=2, max=10s) and NoRetry. With exponential backoff: waits 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200 ms for 5 attempts (about 6.2 s total). Add jitter (random +/-20%) so 10,000 clients do not retry in lockstep and flatten a recovering server (a "retry storm"). Stripe and AWS SDKs document exponential backoff with jitter.

interface RetryPolicy { long delayMs(int attempt); } // attempt starts at 1
class Exponential implements RetryPolicy {
    public long delayMs(int a) { return Math.min(10_000, 200L << (a - 1)); }
}

Everyday analogy. A GPS app letting you pick fastest, shortest or avoid tolls: same map, different algorithm.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Strategy is "just inheritance". It is composition: the context holds a strategy, which can change at runtime.
  • Forgetting statelessness: a strategy shared across threads should be immutable or thread-safe.

notes.title: When NOT to use Strategy
notes.html:
Do not reach for it when:

  • There are two variants and no sign of a third. A boolean parameter is simpler. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It).
  • The variants are different in data, not behaviour. Use a config table or enum with fields: enum Tax { GST(0.18), VAT(0.20) }.
  • The choice happens once at startup and never changes. A constructor argument or DI binding is enough; you do not need a setter.
  • The behaviours share so much code that variants are 2-line differences. Then Template Method (next section) or a parameter fits better.

Cost to name. Each strategy is a class (or lambda), plus a place that selects it. For 3 variants that is about 3 extra files in Java, about 3 lines in Kotlin. Debugging jumps through an interface: "which implementation ran?" needs a breakpoint.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-engineering a toy: "I would make a StringUpperCaseStrategy." Resist.
  • Not knowing the lambda form. In Java 8+ and Kotlin, a one-method strategy is a lambda.

notes.title: Template Method: the idea
notes.html:
Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses fill in specific steps. The base class controls the order ("don't call us, we'll call you"); subclasses override only the varying steps.

Good fit: the steps are always the same sequence, only a few steps differ. Examples: data import (open, parse, validate, save, close), report generation, game turn, test lifecycle.

+------------------------------+
| abstract DataImporter        |
| + run()   <-- final template |
|   open(); parse(); validate();|
|   save(); close();           |
| # parse()    abstract        |
| # validate() hook (default)  |
+--------------+---------------+
               ^
      +--------+---------+
      |                  |
 CsvImporter        JsonImporter

Before: two classes copy-pasted the open/validate/save/close code and differ only in parse. A bug fixed in one (say, forgetting to close the file) stays alive in the other.

After:

abstract class DataImporter {
    public final void run(String path) {          // final: order cannot be broken
        open(path);
        try {
            List<Row> rows = parse();             // varies
            if (validate(rows)) save(rows);       // hook with default
        } finally { close(); }                    // always runs
    }
    protected abstract List<Row> parse();
    protected boolean validate(List<Row> rows) { return !rows.isEmpty(); } // hook
    protected void open(String p) { /* shared */ }
    protected void save(List<Row> r) { /* shared */ }
    protected void close() { /* shared */ }
}
class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    protected List<Row> parse() { /* split by comma */ return List.of(); }
}

Kotlin variant.

abstract class DataImporter {
    fun run(path: String) {            // not open -> cannot be overridden
        open(path)
        try {
            val rows = parse()
            if (validate(rows)) save(rows)
        } finally { close() }
    }
    protected abstract fun parse(): List<Row>
    protected open fun validate(rows: List<Row>) = rows.isNotEmpty()
    private fun open(p: String) {}
    private fun save(r: List<Row>) {}
    private fun close() {}
}

Kotlin classes and methods are final by default, so run is protected from overriding for free; you must write open for hooks.

Decision gravity. Template Method uses inheritance, which is the harder door to walk back: subclasses depend on the base class's step order and protected members (the "fragile base class" problem). Changing the template can silently break every subclass. If you later want to vary two things independently, you will be refactoring into Strategy.

Everyday analogy. A recipe card for "bake a cake": preheat, mix, bake, cool are fixed; the flavour step (chocolate or vanilla) changes.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting final on the template method.
  • Confusing a hook (optional override, has a default) with an abstract step (must override).
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor: the subclass field is not initialised yet.

notes.title: Template Method in real libraries and Android
notes.html:
Where Template Steps you fill in
Android Activity / Fragment lifecycle driven by the framework onCreate, onStart, onResume ...
Android AsyncTask (old) execute() doInBackground, onPostExecute
Android RecyclerView.Adapter binding flow onCreateViewHolder, onBindViewHolder, getItemCount
Android View measure/draw onMeasure, onDraw
Java InputStream read(byte[]) calls abstract read()
Java AbstractList add/iterator built on get(int), size()
JUnit 4 / 5 test run order @Before, @Test, @After
Spring JdbcTemplate open connection, run, close, map errors your row mapper / callback
Servlet HttpServlet service() dispatches doGet, doPost

Worked example (Activity). The system calls onCreate once, onStart and onResume every time the screen comes forward. If you do a 300 ms disk read inside onCreate, the first frame is late (jank above 16 ms per frame at 60 fps). The template tells you where each kind of work belongs; breaking its rules (not calling super.onCreate()) throws SuperNotCalledException.

Template vs Strategy in one line. Template Method varies steps by inheritance (compile time, class level). Strategy varies a whole algorithm by composition (runtime, object level). Modern advice: prefer Strategy or callbacks ("Spring JdbcTemplate + lambda") unless you truly own the framework skeleton.

Everyday analogy. An airline boarding procedure: same order every flight, only the gate and aircraft differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Activity lifecycle is "Observer". It is a Template Method driven by the framework (observers come in via LifecycleObserver).
  • Not calling super in a hook where the base class does vital work.

notes.title: Template Method refactored to Strategy
notes.html:
When subclassing explodes (CsvJsonUtf8Importer, CsvJsonUtf16Importer ...) switch to composition. Same skeleton, but the varying step is injected.

class DataImporter {
    private final Parser parser;                      // the strategy
    DataImporter(Parser p) { this.parser = p; }
    public void run(String path) {
        open(path);
        try { save(parser.parse()); } finally { close(); }
    }
}
interface Parser { List<Row> parse(); }
class DataImporter(private val parse: () -> List<Row>) {
    fun run(path: String) { /* open */ try { /* save */ parse() } finally { /* close */ } }
}

Trade-off table.

Template Method Strategy
Mechanism inheritance composition
Change at runtime no yes
Number of varying parts easy to add hooks, hard to combine each part is its own strategy
Testing need subclass or mock subclass inject a fake
Coupling base-subclass tight interface-only

Everyday analogy. Template = a franchise with fixed store layout and a local manager. Strategy = the same store plugging in whichever supplier you choose.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "always prefer composition" without noting that Template Method is still ideal for framework hooks you do not own.
  • Stating that one is "better". The answer is when: fixed skeleton owned by you -> Template; swappable algorithm -> Strategy.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Behavioral patterns replace conditionals with polymorphism or add indirection between objects.
  • Strategy: same job, interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, picked at runtime. A lambda in Java 8+/Kotlin when it has one method.
  • Use Strategy for growing variants (discount, retry, comparator); skip it for two stable branches or pure data differences.
  • Template Method: base class fixes the order (final template), subclasses fill abstract steps and optional hooks. Android lifecycle, RecyclerView.Adapter, Spring templates are real cases.
  • Template uses inheritance (fragile base class, compile-time); Strategy uses composition (runtime, testable). Refactor Template to Strategy when subclasses multiply.
  • Always show the before (if/else or copy-paste) and the after in interviews, and say what the pattern costs.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Strategy pattern and what problem does it solve?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can name the smell (growing if/else) and the mechanism (interface plus composition), not just recite GoF.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I put each variant of an algorithm behind one interface and let the caller hold a reference to it. Instead of if (type == A) ... else if (type == B) ... inside the caller, I swap the object. New variant means a new class; the caller is not edited. It is Open/Closed in practice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three roles: the context (Checkout), the strategy interface (DiscountStrategy), and concrete strategies (PercentOff, FlatOff). The context delegates one call. The selection of which strategy happens elsewhere (factory, DI, config), so the context stays free of conditionals.

Checkout --has-a--> <<DiscountStrategy>> <|-- PercentOff
                                         <|-- FlatOff

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface DiscountStrategy { double apply(double total); }
class PercentOff implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final double pct;
    PercentOff(double pct) { this.pct = pct; }
    public double apply(double t) { return t * (1 - pct / 100); }
}
class Checkout {
    private final DiscountStrategy discount;
    Checkout(DiscountStrategy d) { this.discount = d; }
    double total(double sum) { return discount.apply(sum); }
}
fun interface DiscountStrategy { fun apply(total: Double): Double }
class Checkout(private val discount: DiscountStrategy) {
    fun total(sum: Double) = discount.apply(sum)
}
val c = Checkout { it * 0.9 }   // lambda as strategy

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Introducing Strategy for two branches that never change.
  • Putting the selection switch inside the context, which defeats the point.
  • Strategies that need different inputs, so the interface grows a pile of unused parameters.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the choice of strategy live? -> In a factory, DI module or config, never in the context.
  2. Can a lambda be a strategy? -> Yes, when the interface has one method; Kotlin function types and Java functional interfaces.
  3. How is it different from State? -> The client picks a Strategy; State objects change themselves as the context transitions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it removes if/else". Senior: adds that the interface shape is the one-way-ish decision, the pattern is reversible and local, and names the cost (extra classes, indirection when debugging).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pricing module with 6 inline discount branches broke twice a quarter on unrelated edits until each rule became a strategy.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the Template Method pattern. Who controls the flow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests inheritance-based reuse understanding and the "Hollywood principle".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A base class defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a final method and calls abstract or hook steps that subclasses fill in. The base class controls the order; subclasses only supply the varying steps. "Don't call us, we'll call you."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The template method is usually final so subclasses cannot reorder steps. Abstract steps are mandatory; hooks have a default (often empty) body and are optional. Typical shape: open -> parse -> validate -> save -> close.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
abstract class DataImporter {
    public final void run() { open(); List<Row> r = parse(); save(r); }
    protected void open() {}              // hook
    protected abstract List<Row> parse(); // required step
    private void save(List<Row> r) { /* common */ }
}
class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    protected List<Row> parse() { return readCsv(); }
}
abstract class DataImporter {
    fun run() { open(); val r = parse(); save(r) }   // final by default
    protected open fun open() {}
    protected abstract fun parse(): List<Row>
    private fun save(r: List<Row>) { /* common */ }
}
class CsvImporter : DataImporter() {
    override fun parse(): List<Row> = readCsv()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving the template method overridable so subclasses break the order.
  • Subclass forgetting super in a hook where the base does vital work.
  • Too many hooks, so nobody understands the skeleton.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Hook vs abstract step? -> Abstract is mandatory, hook is optional with a default.
  2. Why make the template final? -> To protect the invariant sequence.
  3. What is the main cost? -> Tight base/subclass coupling; the fragile base class problem.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines it. Senior adds that it is inheritance (compile time) and that modern code often prefers a callback or Strategy unless you own a real framework skeleton.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Android Activity.onCreate -> onStart -> onResume is a template; forgetting super.onCreate() crashes the app.

questions.promptHtml: Strategy and Template Method both vary behaviour. When do you pick which?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates inheritance-vs-composition judgement from memorised definitions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Template Method varies steps by inheritance, fixed at compile time, with the base class owning the flow. Strategy varies the whole algorithm by composition and can change at runtime. I default to Strategy or a lambda; I use Template Method only when I own a framework skeleton that must enforce a step order.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Template Method Strategy
Mechanism inheritance composition
Binding compile time runtime
Granularity single steps whole algorithm
Testing subclass or mock subclass inject a fake
Coupling base-subclass tight interface only

Refactor path: extract the abstract step into an interface, inject it into the (now concrete) former base class.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing inheritance just to share two lines.
  • Believing Strategy cannot enforce ordering: the context still owns the order.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you combine them? -> Yes: template skeleton in context, steps as injected strategies.
  2. Which is easier to unit test? -> Strategy, no subclass needed.
  3. When is inheritance right? -> Framework-owned lifecycle with enforced ordering and few variants.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states "favour composition" with the test-and-runtime reasons and names the exception.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 5-level importer hierarchy was flattened into one class plus 4 injected parsers; test setup dropped from subclassing mocks to one-line fakes.

questions.promptHtml: Give real examples of Strategy in the JDK or Android, and explain why they count.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you recognise patterns in the code you use daily.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Comparator passed to Collections.sort is the textbook case: same sort algorithm, swappable comparison. In Android, a Hilt-bound interface (real vs fake repository) or RecyclerView.LayoutManager swaps layout behaviour; Retrofit converters and OkHttp Dns are also pluggable policies.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Pattern test: is there one stable caller, one narrow interface, and several interchangeable implementations chosen from outside? Comparator, ThreadPoolExecutor's RejectedExecutionHandler, and Executor all pass. A retry RetryPolicy with delayMs(attempt) is the same shape.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling every interface "Strategy"; a plain callback for one event is not.
  • Forgetting the strategy is injected, not selected by the caller itself.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is RejectedExecutionHandler Strategy? -> Yes, abort/caller-runs/discard are swappable policies.
  2. Strategy vs plain lambda? -> A lambda is Strategy with one method.
  3. How do you test with it? -> Inject a deterministic fake (fixed comparator, zero-delay retry).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links the example to DI and testability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Swapping a RetryPolicy fake with zero delay cut an integration suite from 9 minutes to 40 seconds.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout method is 240 lines with six payment branches. Two bugs this quarter came from edits to one branch breaking another. Product wants a seventh method (BNPL) next sprint.

double pay(Order o, String type) {
    if (type.equals("CARD")) { /* 40 lines */ }
    else if (type.equals("UPI")) { /* 40 lines */ }
    else if (type.equals("WALLET")) { /* 40 lines */ }
    // ... 3 more
    else throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
    return o.total();
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it. Which classes appear, and what changes when BNPL arrives?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split into six private methods." That shortens the method but still edits the same class and if chain for every new type.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do methods need different inputs (card token vs UPI id)? Is the method chosen per request or per user? Is there shared pre/post logic (fraud check, audit)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze edits to the branches; add characterization tests per type before touching.
  3. Approach: Introduce PaymentStrategy { PaymentResult pay(Order o); }, six implementations, and a Map<String, PaymentStrategy> registry wired by DI.
  4. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentStrategy { PaymentResult pay(Order o); }
class CheckoutService {
    private final Map<String, PaymentStrategy> byType;
    CheckoutService(Map<String, PaymentStrategy> m) { this.byType = m; }
    PaymentResult pay(Order o, String type) {
        PaymentStrategy s = byType.get(type);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
        return s.pay(o);
    }
}
fun interface PaymentStrategy { fun pay(o: Order): PaymentResult }
class CheckoutService(private val byType: Map<String, PaymentStrategy>) {
    fun pay(o: Order, type: String) =
        (byType[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException(type)).pay(o)
}
  1. BNPL arrives: one new class plus one registry entry; zero existing lines edited.
  2. Prevention: a test that every enum value has a registered strategy.
  3. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use reflection-based auto-discovery unless there are 20+ strategies; explicit wiring is greppable. Six classes cost indirection when debugging.
  4. Shared logic: keep fraud check and audit in the service, not copied into each strategy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Strategies need different inputs? -> Pass a PaymentRequest context object or sealed request type.
  • Type comes from the client as a string? -> Validate against the registry; unknown type returns 400, not 500.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added a method by copy-pasting a branch and left a hard-coded merchant id; after strategies, each class had its own test file and the mistake was visible in review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: splits into private methods only.
  • Hire: interface, implementations, selection outside the service.
  • Strong hire: registry wiring, shared-logic placement, exhaustiveness test, cost named.

questions.contextHtml: Pricing code has DiscountStrategy with PercentOff and FlatOff. Marketing asks for "buy 3 get cheapest free", which needs the cart lines, not just the total. The current signature is double apply(double total).
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, and how do you avoid breaking existing strategies?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add a second method applyToCart to the interface and throw UnsupportedOperationException in the old classes (an LSP violation).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Will more rules need cart context (user tier, date)? Do rules stack or is exactly one applied?
  2. Immediate mitigation: none needed; this is a design change.
  3. Approach: Change the input to a context object: Money apply(PricingContext ctx) where the context holds total and lines. Old strategies read ctx.total().
  4. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record PricingContext(double total, List<Line> lines) {}
interface DiscountStrategy { double apply(PricingContext ctx); }
class BuyThreeCheapestFree implements DiscountStrategy {
    public double apply(PricingContext c) { /* sort lines, return cheapest */ return 0; }
}
data class PricingContext(val total: Double, val lines: List<Line>)
fun interface DiscountStrategy { fun apply(ctx: PricingContext): Double }
  1. Classes changed: the interface and its two existing implementations (mechanical). The context class stays closed to future rules because new inputs go into PricingContext.
  2. Prevention: keep the context immutable and additive.
  3. Trade-offs: a fat context can leak unused data; the alternative (separate interface per input shape) multiplies types. I pick the context object.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rules must stack? -> Composite of strategies applied in order, or a rule engine if order and conflicts matter.
  • Binary compatibility on a published lib? -> Add a default method delegating the old form.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "simple" interface kept gaining parameters until five of eight arguments were ignored per strategy; a context object ended the churn.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds throwing methods.
  • Hire: context object.
  • Strong hire: names OCP limit of the interface change and stacking implications.

questions.contextHtml:
A rate limiter strategy is a Spring singleton shared by all requests. Under load, some users get wrong "retry after" values. Code:

class BackoffRetry implements RetryPolicy {
    private int attempt = 0;                 // field on a shared singleton
    public long delayMs() { attempt++; return 100L << attempt; }
}

Metrics: p99 retry delay hits 52 minutes at 300 rps; unit tests pass.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized." That makes it thread-safe but still wrong: attempts of different callers share one counter.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the strategy bean singleton or prototype? Does the context own the attempt count?
  2. Immediate mitigation: cap the shift and delay (min(attempt, 10)) as a hotfix.
  3. Root cause: per-call state lives in a shared strategy. State belongs to the caller; the strategy should be stateless: delayMs(int attempt).
  4. Fix:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface RetryPolicy { long delayMs(int attempt); }
class Exponential implements RetryPolicy {
    public long delayMs(int attempt) { return Math.min(30_000, 100L << Math.min(attempt, 8)); }
}
fun interface RetryPolicy { fun delayMs(attempt: Int): Long }
val exponential = RetryPolicy { a -> minOf(30_000L, 100L shl minOf(a, 8)) }
  1. Why tests passed: single-threaded, one caller, counter reset per test.
  2. Prevention: a concurrent test hammering one instance; lint for mutable fields in strategy classes.
  3. Trade-offs: if a strategy truly needs state (token bucket), create one per key and document it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Jitter? -> Inject a Random/clock so tests stay deterministic.
  • Overflow of the shift? -> Cap the exponent as shown.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared strategy singleton quietly mixed counters between tenants; the incident looked like a network problem for a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds synchronized.
  • Hire: moves state to the caller.
  • Strong hire: concurrency test, cap, and rule for stateful strategies.

questions.contextHtml: In code review a teammate wrote ShippingStrategy, FreeShipping, PaidShipping, ShippingStrategyFactory and a config class for one rule: shipping is free over 500. The rule has not changed in three years and has no variants planned.
questions.promptHtml: Do you approve? What do you ask for instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Patterns are good practice, approve." Ignores cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a second rule on the roadmap? Is there a regional variation we know about? Does any test need to fake it?
  2. Decision: request changes. Four types for one comparison is speculative generality.
  3. What I'd ask for: double shipping(double total) { return total > 500 ? 0 : 49; }, with the threshold as a named constant.
  4. Trigger to refactor: the third variant, or runtime selection needed. The refactor is cheap and reversible, so waiting costs little.
  5. Cost of the pattern: each class adds a file, a jump when debugging, and a registry to keep in sync.
  6. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not merely lecture; I would link the rule of three and offer to pair if the variants arrive.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• They say "for testability"? -> A pure function is already testable with no mocks.
  • Rule is likely to change per tenant? -> Then Strategy or config makes sense; ask the product owner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A codebase with 40 single-implementation interfaces made every change a four-file edit; deleting them removed 2k lines with no behaviour change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves by default.
  • Hire: asks for simple code.
  • Strong hire: names the refactor trigger and reversibility.

questions.contextHtml:
A base class calls an overridable hook from its constructor. A subclass NPEs in production only for one subclass.

abstract class Report {
    Report() { init(); }
    protected abstract void init();
}
class SalesReport extends Report {
    private final List<String> cols = new ArrayList<>();   // initialised after super()
    protected void init() { cols.add("region"); }          // NPE
}

Stack trace: NullPointerException at SalesReport.init(SalesReport.java:6).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Initialise cols in init()" which hides the ordering trap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many subclasses? Does init need constructor parameters?
  2. Immediate mitigation: lazy-init the field in the hook as a stopgap.
  3. Root cause: Java runs the superclass constructor before subclass field initialisers, so the hook sees cols == null. Kotlin has the same trap with open members used in init blocks.
  4. Fix: do not call overridable methods from constructors. Expose an explicit final void start() template, or inject the variation (a ColumnProvider) via the constructor.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
abstract class Report {
    public final void build() { init(); render(); }   // called after full construction
    protected abstract void init();
    private void render() {}
}
abstract class Report {
    fun build() { init(); render() }
    protected abstract fun init()
    private fun render() {}
}
  1. Prevention: static analysis rule (Sonar "overridable method called from constructor").
  2. Trade-offs: an explicit build() call means callers must remember it; a factory method hides that.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does only one subclass fail? -> Only that one uses a field in the hook.
  • Final fields? -> Still not yet assigned at that moment.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework base class initialised a view from its constructor; a rare subclass with a field initialiser crashed only in one release channel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches with null checks.
  • Hire: explains construction order.
  • Strong hire: redesigns to explicit template or injection and adds lint.

questions.contextHtml: DataImporter has an abstract parse() with 5 subclasses (CSV, JSON, XML, ...). A test for the shared save logic requires a throwaway subclass, and a new requirement says "choose the parser per file at runtime from the extension".
questions.promptHtml: How do you refactor, and how do you test it after?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add another subclass for each extension and instanceof in the caller", which keeps inheritance and still needs runtime selection.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do subclasses override anything besides parse? Is the importer constructed per file?
  2. Approach: extract interface Parser { List<Row> parse(InputStream in); }; make DataImporter concrete and constructor-inject it; choose by extension in a small registry.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class DataImporter {
    private final Parser parser;
    DataImporter(Parser p) { this.parser = p; }
    public void run(InputStream in) { save(parser.parse(in)); }
    private void save(List<Row> r) {}
}
class DataImporter(private val parser: Parser) {
    fun run(input: InputStream) = save(parser.parse(input))
    private fun save(r: List<Row>) {}
}
  1. Testing: new DataImporter(in -> List.of(row)) verifies save with no subclass; each Parser is tested alone with sample files.
  2. Migration: do it one subclass at a time; old subclass delegates to the new Parser until callers move.
  3. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: if import steps must run in a strict order enforced for all callers, I keep the skeleton in the concrete class (it is still a template, now via composition). I would not do a big-bang rewrite.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Binary compat for external subclasses? -> Deprecate the base for one release.
  • Shared per-parser setup/teardown? -> Add open/close to Parser or use try-with-resources.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Removing a 4-level importer hierarchy let a new format ship in a day instead of a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more subclasses.
  • Hire: Parser interface plus injection.
  • Strong hire: incremental migration, test improvement, skeleton retained where needed.

questions.contextHtml:
After a refactor, 1.8% of sessions crash on launch. Crashlytics: SuperNotCalledException: Activity BaseActivity did not call through to super.onCreate(). A new BaseActivity introduced a protected abstract int layoutId() and overrides onCreate:

override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
    setContentView(layoutId())   // forgot super.onCreate(b)
}

Rollout is at 20% of users.
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate, find the root cause, and prevent a repeat.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fix the line only; no rollout action and no guard for the next base class.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which versions and devices? Is the staged rollout pausable? Did tests run through instrumentation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: halt the staged rollout; roll back or hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses: missing super, a subclass overriding without super, lifecycle ordering.
  4. Verify: stack trace points at BaseActivity; unit tests with Robolectric Robolectric.buildActivity(...).create().
  5. Root cause: Activity.onCreate is a Template Method hook that framework code requires to be called; our own override replaced it without chaining.
  6. Fix: call super first, and apply our own template: make onCreate final in BaseActivity and expose protected abstract fun layoutId() and an optional open fun onReady().
  7. Prevention: lint rule MissingSuperCall, a launch smoke test per Activity in CI.
  8. Trade-offs: final template protects order but limits subclasses; prefer composition (lifecycle observers) for cross-cutting needs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just remove BaseActivity? -> Often right; use DefaultLifecycleObserver.
  • Staged rollout metrics? -> Gate on crash-free sessions threshold.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A base class change slipped because only one screen was tested manually; a launch-every-Activity smoke test caught the next one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes line only.
  • Hire: halts rollout, explains template hook.
  • Strong hire: final template, lint, CI smoke test, composition alternative.

questions.contextHtml: A notification-ranking feature uses three algorithms (recency, relevance, ML-based). Product wants A/B experiments choosing the algorithm per user, with a kill-switch, and QA needs deterministic tests.
questions.promptHtml: Design the class model and testing approach.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: if (flag.isEnabled("ml")) ... else ... scattered through the feed code.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is assignment sticky per user? Fallback if ML times out? Is the choice per request or per session?
  2. Model: RankingStrategy interface; RankingSelector takes a User and flag provider and returns a strategy; FeedService receives the selector via DI.
  3. Failure handling: wrap ML in a FallbackRanking(primary, recency) decorator with a timeout.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface RankingStrategy { List<Item> rank(List<Item> items, User u); }
class RankingSelector {
    private final Map<String, RankingStrategy> all; private final Flags flags;
    RankingSelector(Map<String, RankingStrategy> a, Flags f) { all = a; flags = f; }
    RankingStrategy forUser(User u) { return all.getOrDefault(flags.variant(u), all.get("recency")); }
}
fun interface RankingStrategy { fun rank(items: List<Item>, u: User): List<Item> }
class RankingSelector(private val all: Map<String, RankingStrategy>, private val flags: Flags) {
    fun forUser(u: User) = all[flags.variant(u)] ?: all.getValue("recency")
}
  1. Testing: inject a fake selector returning a fixed strategy; test each strategy as a pure function; test the selector with a fake Flags.
  2. Kill-switch: unknown or disabled variant falls back to recency.
  3. Trade-offs: selection logic is now one class to audit; I would not read flags inside strategies.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Experiment metrics? -> Tag each response with the variant used.
  • ML strategy is slow? -> Timeout then fallback; log the fallback rate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An experiment flag read in four places let users see inconsistent rankings in one session; centralising selection fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flag checks inline.
  • Hire: strategy plus selector plus DI.
  • Strong hire: fallback decorator, sticky assignment, test seams.
